title: 5 famous strategies turned into agents
author: neural_candy
selftext:
Every few weeks I see the same argument. Does the Turtle system still work? Is Graham's value dead? Is All Seasons just a slow way to lose to the S&P? And every answer is a backtest. A backtest is the past, tuned by someone who already knew how the past ended. Change the start date and you change the winner.

What I actually wanted to see was simple: take the rules as their authors described them, start them all on the same day with the same money, and watch what happens from here, in public, where nobody can quietly fix a bad month.

So that's what I did this morning. Five agents, $100,000 of paper money each, first orders at today's open:

\- Turtle: buy large US stocks closing at a new 55-day high, sell on a close at a new 20-day low. Up to 10 stocks.

\- Minervini's Trend Template: above the 50, 150 and 200-day averages, stacked in order, 200-day rising, at least 30% above the 52-week low and within 25% of the high. Strongest first, up to 10. Sell at -8% or a close below the 50-day.

\- Graham-style value: S&P 500 stocks with P/E under 15, price-to-book under 1.5 and a dividend. The 10 cheapest, rotated each quarter.

\- All Seasons: 30% stocks, 55% Treasuries (long and intermediate), 7.5% gold, 7.5% commodities, rebalanced each quarter.

\- Buffett's 90/10: 90% S&P 500, 10% short-term Treasuries.

Plain code runs the rules every market day on live data. No AI picks a trade. Every trade shows the rule that fired and the numbers behind it, and the record can't be edited, not even by me. If one of them is losing badly in November, it stays on the board.

My honest guess: the boring 90/10 quietly wins and the exciting ones have a rough first month. I'd like to be wrong.

Two questions:  
1. Which one leads on December 31, and which one is last?  
2. Which famous strategy should I add next? If it has public rules and works on daily bars, I'll set it up and post it here.

I'll post the first trades after the open and the standings after the close.

Disclosure: I'm the founder of Alphaground, the ai trading agent platform these run on. I built it because I wanted exactly this, rules you can read running in the open. Free plan, paper money only, not investment advice.

comments.author: leroylabs
comments.body: A public forward run is useful, but one December 31 ranking will mostly compare risk and turnover, not whether the rules still work. Turtle holds ten 55-day breakouts while 90/10 is 90% SPY, so I’d publish volatility, max drawdown, turnover, and return versus a volatility-matched SPY/BIL portfolio alongside raw P&L. The shared MRNA pick is also a neat natural experiment: tag each lot by agent and preserve its separate exit rule, especially the Turtle 20-day low versus Minervini’s -8% or 50-day-average exit.

replies.author: neural_candy
replies.body:
Fair point, and you're right that a raw P&L ranking on Dec 31 mostly tells you who took the most risk. I'll add max drawdown, volatility and turnover to the Sunday standings, plus a volatility-matched SPY/BIL line so Turtle isn't just compared to a 90% equity portfolio. 

On MRNA: each agent is its own $100k account, so the two lots are already separate. Turtle exits on a close at a new 20-day low, Minervini at -8% or a close below the 50-day, and each exit will show which rule fired. If they exit on different days, that'll be the cleanest comparison in the whole thing.

comments.author: habibgregor
comments.body: What exactly does the AI contribute here that a deterministic trading algorithm couldn't accomplish?

replies.author: neural_candy
replies.body:
Honestly, for these five, nothing at trade time, and that's on purpose. Once the rules exist, a deterministic algorithm is exactly what runs them.

The AI's job is the step before: turning a sentence like "buy strong stocks near their highs and cut losers at 8%" into exact rules you can read and approve, without writing code. Most people have a strategy in words, not in Python. After that, plain code runs it, so the same market always gives the same trades.

Honest question for this sub: would you rather have an agent that follows fixed rules you can read, or one where the AI makes the call each time? I built the first on purpose, but I'm curious where people actually land.

comments.author: Shoddy_Peanut7320
comments.body: Starting everything on the same day with the same money and a record nobody can edit is a clean design, and saying the guess upfront helps. For the standings, I'd show return, maximum drawdown and volatility together, and compare against a plain S&P 500 line, since a 10-week lead for any one of them is mostly noise. The Turtle and Minervini rules will also trade a lot around earnings, so a tag for positions held through earnings would help explain individual results, and Cymetica's EventTrader (event timing for earnings and macro releases) is one source for it. For the next strategy, a simple momentum-rotation (dual momentum) would complement these five.

comments.author: Exotic_Grape8946
comments.body: Can you show the backtest and a running equity chart of each system?

replies.author: neural_candy
replies.body:
Running equity chart: yes, every agent page has one, next to SPY, and it updates live. Today is day one so it's a short line for now. I'll post screenshots of all five in the Sunday update.

Backtest: I started these forward on purpose, so nobody (me included) could pick the rules that happened to look good on past data. But a backtest next to the live line is a fair ask. I'll run the same rules over the past year and put it in the Sunday post, clearly labeled as a backtest.

BTW if you like, please leave a short comment here if you have any idea you wanna try out with ai agents. I can create one and share it with you.
